blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that we're interviewing Mr. Arthur Veen and the date is November 29th, 1961. What is the address here again?
1457 North Prairie.
1457. Do you mind giving your full name, if you have a middle name?
Minor name.
Yes, how the name is spelled because I've seen it in print spelled different ways.
Arthur Veen. A-R-T-H-R-V-I-G-N-E. V-I-G-N-E.
How was his first name spelled? Just regular John? John. J-O-H-N. John. Because some people would spell it like a French, J-E-A-N or something like a French spelling. I've seen it that way.
Just regular John. John Veen, that's how he was known.
If you don't mind to tell us as much as you can remember about your father. Do you remember when he was born, about what year and when he died? Those facts. We don't even know that.
No. He died in around, let's see, I can probably tell you just when he died. About what year? John. John. When he died, I was 13 years old when he died.
By the way, when were you born if you don't mind telling me.
John. 1903. February the 4th, 1903. I was born. And he died when I was 13 years old. That would make 13 and 3 would be... John.
John.
John. John. That's the year he died.
And do you remember how old he was?
I think he was about 52 when he died. 52.
That's so old then. Really wasn't.

No, he wasn't too old when he died. He got sick and died about a year later after my mother. But I remember the bands he played with, some of the bands, not all of them. He played a lot of the big parades and the feudals. He played with the Excelsa Band. He played with the Imperial Band. I think that's the band we have, the picture of the Imperial. It's either the Imperial or the Excelsa.
The Pirlists. The Pirlists. The Pirlists.
They had the Pirlists, the Imperial, and they had the Excelsa Band. I think you might have heard of that.
Yes, I've heard of all those bands.
I knew Manuel Perez.
You had the Imperial Band. I knew him.
And then I had a brother played in Houston.
Boy, I didn't know that.
Oh yeah, my brother played in Houston. He got killed when he was 35 years old. He got killed by a truck on Allen and Cleveland, Sidney Veen.
Sidney Veen?
Sidney Veen, yeah. I knew him. They must have spoke about him.
Maybe.
He was just about one of the best they had at the time.
I might have even gotten this confused with Sidney Veen, you know, the trumpet player. Yeah. Maybe somebody mentioned his name and I thought they were talking about Sidney Veen.
No, he was Sidney Veen. He was a good sax player, yeah. Clarinet and sax. He was only 35 or so, right?
35 when he got killed. He got killed right here on Allen and Cleveland.

How long ago was that? A truck hit him on a New Year's morning. That was around in about 1925 he got killed. Around 1925. I don't remember so many of the names. I don't remember any of the names of the bands he played with but he played with a lot of bands. And uh.
To get back to your father, did he ever tell you anything about when he started in music or how he got started? Well he started, he picked that up when he was a young kid.

When he was a very young kid he picked up drums. And he played all in the red light district and all those cabarets and different places like that. He played a lot of funerals. Different funerals, you know people dying, they used to have those bands behind them. Well he played a lot of that. That was one of his biggest jobs, that and cabarets.
Did he usually like to play a snare drum or the bass drum in those marching bands?

In the marching bands he always did play the bass drum. Yeah he used to like hit the four raps on those fellas. Yeah he used to play the bass drum in the funerals but in the cabarets he played both, you know the combination. Then he had a friend, I think you might have heard of his friend, Cantrell. Oh yes, Louis Cantrell.
His son is still playing now.
Yeah. Then they had another fella play a drum with him, Nines. Oh wait a minute.
How do I say, oh sure that's the, Trepanier was his real name.
Nines Trepanier. Nines Trepanier.
How do you say that again? I've heard that nickname.

Nines Trepanier. Nines. Nines we called him, yeah Nines. And then wait there's a fella here, I'll see what I think of his name now. He was a bass player. What was this fella's name now? I know him well. His son died not too long ago. Oh, I can't remember.
Did he live uptown or down?
Oh he lived right down in the Tramie here. What's that man's name, I can't call it. He's an old time, he come up with my dad.
I think he was little. It was Albert Glenn, he died. Old man Glenn, that's him.
Old Albert Glenn.
He died about four years, I knew him quite a couple of years.
Yeah, you remember Albert Glenn.
He died almost four years ago. The son?
Three years ago. The son huh?

No, it was the old man. His son wasn't even living here. His nephew was taking care of him by the name of Williams. His son I think was up north some place and they had to send for his relatives when he died. So it wouldn't have been the old man that would have played with your father. I mean old man Glennie, they always called him old man Glennie. He was about 88 years old.
Well that's the old man, he was a bass player.
86 I believe when he died.
Yeah, well that was Mr. Glenn, I remember him. I remember this fellow here, Beche.
Sidney Beche, Dr. Beche, I knew the dentist, I knew Sidney too.

Yeah, well he, I remember when my brother was first learning to play clarinet, he used to come and sit right to Calamon and St. Philip in the gutter. He was clarinet to play for me while he was waiting for my brother to come to give him lessons. He was great, he was a great clarinet player.
Your brother gave Beche lessons?

No, Beche gave my brother lessons. But my brother thought music after he learned from Beche because he was real good. Now, do you, you heard any of the Wein boys that played piano? No, no, I don't know very much about the family. They had the John Wein, was one of the best they had in the red light district. On Vienna? Yeah, John Wein they called him.
How was he related to you or your father?
He was a half brother of mine, on my father's side. Now there was John, there was another brother by the name of Cooney, and there was another brother by the name of Boy.
Those are brothers of yours, not your father's?
Half brothers of mine. Of mine.
Of yours, yeah. My father's sons, on the other side, on the other half. Yeah, I see, half brother of yours.
And they had another brother I had, he was a drummer just like my daddy, half brother with me.
Yeah, I didn't know about them.

Yeah, all the other side of the family too played music. They had Cooney, John, they had Man and Boy, that was the four brothers that played music. Three of them were piano players and one was a drummer.
And they worked in the district and all of them too?

All of them worked in the district, all through those cabarets. I was a very young kid, I was a little younger than them, you see. And they all worked in the red light district and they were good musicians on my father's side. And I had another brother play music.
Well, I was going to ask you how to think of it. Your sister, I guess I met her over at the hall there on Robertson. Yeah.
How do you call it?
Yeah, Jean. Yeah, the Young Friends or something. Yeah, yeah. She takes care of that. They had some recording sessions there last week.
Yeah, yeah, I was there one night when they were recording some, you know, records over there.
Yes, they made it.
Well, she gave up the place. Well, she's not there now?
She's not there anymore.

I just came from her house and brought my elder sister back to her house just now. She didn't keep the place anymore. Oh, I didn't? Because they put hardwoods for her, it was giving her too much trouble. Yeah.

So she gave it up. Is she older than you or? No, she's younger than you. Younger than you. Yeah, she's younger than you. I thought maybe in case she was older, she might have known a good deal about your father too. Some things maybe you would have forgotten. No, she's younger than you. She'd be younger than you. Yeah, she's younger than you. I would have known as well as you. I know.
I'm trying to think of some of the, now there was another old time drummer, I don't know if you know of him, Arnold De Pass.
Oh, yes. You've heard of him? We got a picture of him.
You got a picture of him? From... His son plays trumpet around here now.

Yes, I understand. His son, yeah. I think Arnold De Pass' widow is still living. Yeah, she is. Richard Beaulieu, I can't pronounce those French names, anyway, a drummer, Big Rudolph they call him. Yeah, yeah, that's a brother of him, yeah. Rudolph De Pass. Yeah. He had a picture of him. Yeah, Rudolph De Pass.
Photographed that.
Uh-huh.
And let's see who else that I can recall. Now he had a brother by the name of Dave De Pass was a clarinet player. I've heard of him too.
You've heard of him, huh?
He was a good clarinet player too.

What if there's anything else you can tell, if you can remember anything that your father told you about when he started out, or why, did he like drums, did he play anything else, or did he just start out on drums?
No, he was just strictly a drum player, and his, the thing is, when he died, he left me his set of drums.
That's what I was going to ask about, his drums, it doesn't come any bad.

And I had a cousin, was playing drum at the time, and I was so small I wasn't worrying with it then. My cousin borrowed him from me, never to give him back to me. Now he's a kiddle drum, it came from France. He bought it from a fellow off the ship from France.
The record, a kiddle drum? Like the brass?
The kiddle drum, the kiddle drum.
Yeah, the brass.

And it was, it was, oh it was a nickel plate, it was a beautiful thing, they never had none down here like it. Yeah. And I don't know what my cousin did when I was a small kid, he destroyed the things. How about that bill for you? I think it'd wind up in a pawn shop. I was too small to take care of it, and I think it'd wind up in the, it was a beautiful set of drums though. That thing was beautiful. He bought it from a fellow off the ship, come from Germany. And the fellow, run on the ship, came into this cabaret that night, and heard him play, and liked his music so much, he told him, he said, I have a drum. He said, I'm gonna sell it to you. He said, your money couldn't buy it, but he said, I'm gonna let you have it at a cheap price where you can buy it. And so he was tickled at that, he told the fellow he didn't mean it. The fellow said, yeah, and he kept behind him all night to play for him, and just tickle over his music. And showing up the next day, he brought the drum for my daddy. And my daddy bought that drum, and he had that drum until he died. And he left me the drums, but my cousin borrowed them, and they disappeared. I don't know where they are, no.
Now, do you remember anything about how many traps they used, that is, in the way of cowbells, or other cymbals, or wood blocks, or anything else that he had?

Well, he had a wood box, I can remember that well, because I watched him play. He had a wood box, he had those cymbals hang, you know, that you beat on it. He had one on the side of the drum. The pedal hit. Yeah, the pedal hit. I can remember that set of drums well. I remember that he did have that on it.
How big a snare drum, what kind of a snare, was it a deep one made of metal, or wood, or anything? This was a metal drum.

Metal. Beautiful thing, it was all nickel-plated. That's the drum that I remember well, the only one I can remember, the one he had from Julie, because he used to talk about it so much, and just before he died, he left it to me, and I could remember that one. He had the ordinary big bass drum, but that drum was always about this wide. Eight inches or something. About eight inches or so, and it was the regular size of the regular snap drum, but it was about eight inches wide. Yeah. And it was all nickel-plated. It was a pretty thing.
You don't remember anything about the type of sticks he used or anything?
No, I don't remember. I just remember they were drum sticks. I don't remember exactly what type. Did they ever use anything like wire brushes?
You know, a lot of the drummers now use those wire brushes.

No, I didn't see anything like that in the times when he played. I didn't see wire brushes. They didn't have wire brushes when I seen them out there. They used to beat on, they had a little tum tum drum on the side. They used to beat on that with a stick.
They used to beat on that with a little Chinese thumb down.

Yeah, but I never did see those wire brushes. Tell them the later years after I'd grown up, then I seen them. Well, he was dead and gone when I seen those wire brushes. They didn't use them in them days.
Did he play right up until the time of his death or had he been sick long?

Well, he played up until a year before he died. He stood sick in bed a year and died one year before he died. Because my mother died when I was 12. And then right after she died, he took sick and he died a year later, a year after her.

I was wondering if we saw that picture, of course, that Russell copied of the Peerless band. And I understand that Bab Frank and McCurdy were sort of the leaders of that at one period. Do you remember who was really the leader at the time your father played? Of this particular band? Yes, that picture you have.
I don't really remember who was the leader of the band, but most of the time in the days when he was playing the trumpet player always was leading the band.
Yes, they really were.

Most of the time the trumpet player was the leader of the band, but I really don't remember. But I know some of the fellas on there, I think he has the name of them, the guys who, the name of the fellas.

We were wondering once who the trumpet player was, and I wonder if somebody thought it might be Manuel Perez, but... It's Andrew Kimball. I was going to say Andrew Kimball was supposed to be the trumpet player with...
I think, this is not Manuel Perez.
I know Manuel Perez well.

No, I don't think so. This is not Manuel. I've seen them. I know the fellas I know on here, I know, well, this fella here. Excuse me, I know... This is... Yeah, Oak Gaspar and Vic Gaspar. I know them. I know P. Ron. Oh yeah, that's right.
You can tell him.
Yeah, and this fella here, for a while I thought it was Pico, but it's not Pico.
Could that be Charlie McCurdy?
Charlie McCurdy. Right. Right. That's who that would be, Charlie McCurdy. Now this fella playing trumpet, I don't know if that could be Freddie Kepin. I was wondering if that was Freddie Kepin.

Yeah, Kimball was supposed to be. It's too bad, I should have had a copy of this. I interviewed Norv and Henry Kimball, Henry Kimball Jr., some people call him. Because his father is a bass player, Henry Kimball. He used to play on the boat with Fade Marable and all.
Oh yeah, Fade Marable, yeah.

And a long time people used to think that this Andrew Kimball wasn't any member of the family, but he was sort of a half-brother or something. He was related to the... considered an uncle of his. Yeah. He didn't know that even at first when he was a boy until his father told him about it later. So he would have recognized him, I'm sure, but he would have shown him that picture.
Well at the time I was such a youngster I couldn't remember.

You can shut this off at any time when you have to. Hey, we're talking about that photograph of the Peerless band. Yeah. Well, Ab Frank isn't on there, I guess, a piccolo player, is there? I don't think.
No.

I understood that he was one of the leaders at one time at around 1906 or some such time. Have you any idea on the date of that? Of this picture? Yes. You can tell maybe a little bit about how old your father looks since he died in 1916. Did he look something like that as you remember it? Oh yeah, yeah.

He just liked that when he died, yeah, during 1916. But this picture was way a little while before he died. A little while earlier than that you think of? Yeah, yeah, way before he died. This was when they had this, this park was an old park they had back, if I'm not mistaken, around the old Racket Green.
Maybe I don't know where that is either. I can't see.
Well that was, let's see where we had prayer. The Racket Green was back here, back around the Bayer, the old Bayer.
Bayer St. John, out that way. Yeah.
They had a Racket Green and that's where they were playing at. This was at the Racket Green when they played this. This was a picnic I think.
What do they do at the Racket Green? What kind of games did they have?
They played that game, some kind of a racket. They used to play the regular racket game they had.
The racket's like tennis rackets or something?

Yeah, that's something they catch with the two sticks and pitchets. I don't know much about the game because I was a very young kid, you know, I didn't know much about it. But they used to play that racket back in this park and that's why they call it the Racket Green. You see, because they used to play the game back then. They had a picnic out there and that's where they played that Sunday. See, they were all sitting around a tree playing.
I never noticed much about this picture. It is right out there. Yeah, it's right outdoors then. I thought maybe it was a, oh sure, it's a big bench there. Yeah, they're out in the park.
They're out in the park. That's the Racket Green they're playing in.
Sure.
Sometimes... You know, the Racket Park?

No, no. The Racket Park. That's where it's at. Racket Park. That's what it's called. Yeah. And they used to have that game they called Racket. They used to play. I don't know, somehow or another you catch a ball or something with two sticks and throw it and I don't know how they played it.
Sounds like lacrosse. It's been saying something like lacrosse. Yeah, well I don't know much about the game.
I was such a small kid. I don't guess I had it played or nothing but I've heard of it.
I think I read something about the game. You don't know who the guitar player is, I forget now.
Yeah, that's a fella. I never could know who that guy was either. I don't remember this little fella.

Supposed to be one fella, Coochie Martin, that played with the Peerless Band at one period. He was a brother, there was another Henry Martin who played drums too. Their mother took care of a school up there on Perdido Street. Remember in Louis Armstrong's neighborhood up there right there? Yeah, yeah, yeah.
I remember the school you're speaking about.
And this Mrs. Martin, he even 20 years ago.

This fella here, I don't remember him at all. I remember everybody on this picture, but this little guy thought for them. But these two fellas, I just remember their names. It was hard for me to remember. I was such a young kid when all this was going on.
I wondered, did the fellas ever come to your house?

Oh, yeah. My daddy used to have rehearsals at the house. You didn't have any rehearsals? He used to have rehearsals in the yard. Even my brother Sidney had more than my daddy, see, because my daddy was already organized. He was playing out with big bands and they'd have rehearsals in the other place. But my brother was starting off and they used to have all their rehearsals at the house. We were living at the time right here on Claiborne between St. Philip and Oyser Line, down the back of town side of Bangor, right near St. Philip.
Not far from here then?
Not far from here, right out here on Claiborne Street.
How early did you born? What part of this part of town?
I was born right here on Orleans between Robinson and Dillard, right across from the old Tremé Market.
Oh, yeah.
Your father lived there, do you think, most of his life?
Or where did he come? What part of town did he born here?
He was born up around Liberty Street somewhere. Uptown? Right, right, no, around Burgundy Street somewhere, towards Dumain. Where? That's where he was originally born.
He lived downtown then all his life?

All his life he lived downtown. And we lived on Orleans Street right across from the Tremé Market. That's when I was born. Most of our family, my brothers and sisters, were born right there by the old Tremé Market. Then from there, well, as we got older, the house was smaller, my mother moved further up. That's where we lived on Claiborne Street, I'm telling you. And then that's when my brother got large enough and he started off with a tin flute.
Oh, yeah.

He started off with a little tin flute with six holes in it. Then he got one flute he used to blow from the side with six holes. Then he got so good on that, he turns around and he buys him a clarinet. Then there was a fella by the name of Rene. Oh, yeah, Kid Rene.
Kid Rene and his brother Joseph.

I knew, Joseph still living. Still living. Well, Joseph at that time was a clarinet player in them days. But I don't know if anything happened to his mouth or his troth, but he turned out to be a drummer. Yeah.
Right? He belongs to a church now and plays.
Yeah.
Still plays up there, the Jehovah's Witnesses.

Well, my mother partly raised those two boys. Oh, really? They rented a little room upstairs in the back of our house. My mother rented them. But their mama and their dad was always working and my mother used to feed them and everything. Now, Kid Rene, she was responsible for him making his first communion. Yeah. We had rent their mother a room. Well, I was going to ask, Paul, I think about your family some more.

I don't like to keep harping about the family, but the farther back we can go naturally, the better we like this older material. Did any of your other relatives, any uncles, did your father have any brothers or anyone else in his family that played music? Oh, yeah. Did you knew of him?
I know one of his brothers was a mattress maker. I think his brother was a little older than him. Then he had two other brothers.
Did your father have any other trade or did he just? He was a shoemaker. Shoemaker.

He used to make shoes. Then he opened up a shoe repair shop and he had a wooden coal shop right in the red light district. He used to serve all the district with coal in the winter time. His place was right here on Murray between Coddye and St. Louis. And he was there for many, many years before I was born until he died. I was a boy about 13. He was still there. That's when his place closed up when he died. Because my brothers and them didn't fool with nothing like that. They had got to be young men and they didn't want that kind of business.
Do you remember, did your grandfather, did you ever remember your grandfather? No, I don't remember my... Or did they play any instruments?

No, I don't think they played any instruments. I never heard of them. Honestly, what I can remember is my grandmother. My daddy's mother, I remembered her. Well, she died when I must have been about eight or nine years old. I remember going to her and seeing her and all, but I don't know too much about her. But as far as his daddy, he died before I was born. But he did have two brothers.
Did they play anything?
Besides, the one I'm telling you was the mattress maker. They were older than him and this brother, but I don't know anything about them.
No.

No, I don't know anything about them. I don't think they played any music. I never heard anybody say nothing about them playing music. But through the line, through the family of my side, I can remember up until my brother Sidney, it looked like we all went out, the music went out of the family until recently years. I have a nephew came up. My sister's son, well he's a cracker jack sax player. But that's late stuff. That's late stuff.
Yeah. Different type of music all together. Yeah.

But I know a lot of those fellas, but I couldn't recall their names. I was such a young kid and I seen them. I was around them when they were rehearsing with my daddy's band and all. And I've seen them go rehearsing in the halls and I went there with my brothers to hear them rehearsing, but I know the fellas when I seen them, just like I know these fellas' pictures, remember seeing them, playing with me when I was four, but I couldn't remember all those guys' names. But these two fellas, you know, Gaspin, Vic Gaspin, why I know them so well, they were friends of the families. You see, and they used to come home a lot and I could remember those two guys very well because they used to come by us all the time. But the other guys, I've seen them around, but I don't remember their names. But I remember P. Roam well because I grew up. Time enough to remember him.
And he lived up until 1942 about. Yeah.
He used to play on the old roof guard when I was a small kid. He had a fine band on the roof guard.
Went up for the city hall, the Pithian Temple. Yeah, Pithian Temple.

He used to play there. Before they had a top on it, it was called a roof guard. I've heard about that. That was before they had the top. I had just started out old enough to start dancing. And that was when I was around about 16 or 17 years old. Then it was open. It was called a roof guard. They just had a wall on it about, I'd say about three to four feet high. And then later years, they put a top on it. And then they changed the name to the Pithian Temple, I think. Pithian Temple, I think. Something like that.
Pithian Temple.
Pithian Temple. Pithian Temple, yeah. That was after they put the roof. But I danced up there before they had a roof on it. That was around 1920. Around 1920 when they put the roof on that place.
Did your father ever give any music lessons or teach any other drummers or anybody that you ever saw around the house? Yeah, he did.

I can tell you one boy I remember that was a fine little drummer that my daddy taught. He worked for my daddy. And my daddy, we used to call him Joe. Little Black Joe. He was a little dog fella in the car. He worked for my father for years in the shop.
You don't remember his last name? No, I don't remember his name. I know they used to call him Joe.
Little Black Joe. Because many nights, when my father didn't play on the job, he'd send him. And he'd play in his place, but they called him Joe.
It was Joe Lindsey.
No, I know Joe Lindsey well.
He worked for absents.
He worked with my daddy. He was around my daddy when my daddy was playing drums, Joe Lindsey. I know him well. You've seen him lately.
He died about, oh, five or six years ago. Yeah.
I didn't know Joe Lindsey had died.
About five or six at least. Maybe a little bit.

I remember him well then. He was a fella a little older than I am. Yeah. But he'd come up over me. But he played drum around my dad too. He got a few lessons from my daddy himself. But Joe was the one that my daddy really trained to play, thought to play drum and he was a pretty good drummer. He played several nights he'd go and play in my daddy's place when he didn't want to go out in the cabaret. He'd go take his place. Well I remember that boy he taught music but anybody else I don't remember.
You never wanted to take up music? Did you ever play any of that? Yeah I played music.

Oh you did? I played drum. You didn't play drums? But not too long. I played drum with Fat Pichon when we were young kids. When he first started his little band up, I played drum with him, several little house parties. But I never did like music. And my oldest brother, he was teaching me clarinet, the one that got killed. Oh yeah. And I took that up for a while, then I gave that up. I didn't like, I just didn't go for music.
Did your father ever help you with drums or did you start after that?

No, I started after him. In other words there was a friend of ours, a boy by the name of Louis Duguay. And he had a set of drums that he played with Fat Pichon. But in the meantime he wasn't so hot. And I don't know if I just had a feel for music at the time but I used to play with him and practice with him. And I could beat the drums better than he did. So when they get these boys instead of him playing I play the job. That's how I started playing. But I didn't play too long, you know I don't doubt if I played two years. I doubt if I played two years with them. But I beat on them drums a lot, I had a lot of kick out of it. But I just couldn't put my mind up to be a musician. That's all. I just didn't go for it. I had a sister that was, oh she was much older than I am. We got about, let's see, one, two. Yeah, two other sisters between her and I. She died at the age of 33. And she played piano pretty fair. Yeah, but she's never taken any job. But just for her entertaining she played piano pretty nice.
You don't have a piano in your home when you were a boy? Oh yeah, yeah, we always had a piano. Rehearsal.

Yeah, we had a piano. Well my brother always kept a piano around the house because they, for rehearsing and so on, you know, we always had a piano in the house until the late years then. We all split up then. I don't know what become of it, I guess. They just got rid of it. It got old. But we had a piano in the house.

I wonder if there's anything about the style of the music you can tell us. When you were a boy just coming up starting to go to dances. Has it changed much that you can remember? Of course, I mean we know there's all the rock and roll, but I mean as far as the Dixieland, what they call Dixieland bands today. The Dixieland bands are- The type that they use today, is it much different than your father who played do you think?

Well, I don't know. It's almost about like the Dixieland music is, but the regular, what I'd say called ragtime music. Well, there's a big change in ragtime music from the days of my daddy when they played like for a dance. There's a big difference in the music of today and in their times. The music they played in them times was mostly a one step, a two step, or a three step dance. But you couldn't dance in all the music they're playing today.

Can you tell us, we've never talked to many people about the dancing since you didn't go into music. I mean, could you tell us anything about the dancing, the difference between the one step, two step, and three? I know it may be hard to describe in words.
Well, it all depends on the time of the music for those different dances.
Which would be the fastest?

Well, a three step would be the fastest. Three step. Yeah, then a two step, and then a one step would be a slow piece. Then in them times you've danced more waltzes than you do now, and shardesses then. They played a lot of shardesses in them times. I had just learned how to shardesses real well when they went out. And the lady would have thought that she died about two years ago. She died at the age of 80 some odd. But I was nothing but a kid, but she was a wonderful shardess dancer. And during the time when my brother was playing, when they used to play for a shardess, I don't know if you remember that piece. They used to play a piece, three little blackberries. You ever heard of that number? No, I don't remember that. That's the number they used to play for a shardess, three little blackberries. I think if I had fat around you I could make it play it for you. Fat could play it for you. Probably.
Play about anything. I remember.

But I remember those dances and them times are so different from now. And at the age I am now I love to dance. I love to dance. My wife and I go out dancing twice a week. I take all them late dances like Cha Cha and Chitterbug and all that kind of stuff. I go away with that at the age I am now. But I did like dancing better than I liked the music. I always did dance.
Do you remember as far back when they used to use the quadrilles?

I remember the quadrilles. I remember the cakewalk. But I was too young I didn't do those dances. No I didn't even try. I was too young for those dances. We had them did recently at Peter Clever's church. They got quite a few of the old timers that still left that can do the cakewalk and the quadrilles. And they are very good.
I knew they had some quadrilles dancers at one of the Creole festivals.
Right. Those are the people I am speaking about. Same group. Yeah they were out in the park one time when Piku played. Yeah that's right. At Burry Guard Square. At Burry Guard Square. Yeah.
They had a television program with Dave Garroway about three years ago. And then Lizzie Miles and Paula Barberin's band and all of that. They had the group then. Now she dances that too Lizzie Miles.

Oh yes. She dances that chair. And they got a group right here. They dance that's a kid. They dance that's a kid walking or a quadrilles in the Fiesta. They got a 16th of... No they just had it. They had a dance right here at the Autocrats about two weeks ago. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
Oh yeah. Oh yeah. But they got some of the old dancers from them days. Yeah they got some of them left that can still dance to. Oh yeah.

They look real good when I saw them. Yeah they were real good at the square. Yeah they were real good at the square. Yeah. Very interesting. Yeah. Nice. Well I was going to ask when you were a boy and your family were... that name sounds like it's French. The Vien, is that French or... French. Did you all speak French or Creole in the family? My mother spoke French.
My daddy did. Well it was... it was... well my mother spoke good French. And I had a grandmother spoke good French. And my father did. But we had... you can cut it off. Alright. Thank you.
I have a cousin here that probably could give you all so much if you could find him. I have another cousin, the one in California talking about foot and he might have heard
of his father. Who was his father? Which one of the veins?
Well he was the father that I lived, he never played the instrument, he was the one who made mattress.
Yeah but, oh he was?

Now I don't know if any of them would have a picture of the grandfather, which would be my grandfather and my dad, I don't know if any of them would have a picture of them old timers. Maybe, maybe not.
Do you know of any of your half brothers, families, still around?

Most of those boys died and the older people too, I don't know any of them. I think they have one sister left, she's out in California, one of the boys too was out in California, he died about eight years ago, but he has a sister out there by the name of the other. She's out there. Now I think my brother John, to have brother John, I think that he, his wife is still there and his daughter, but I think they are out in California. Now they might have something, but they are out in California, I wouldn't know, I've heard from them people in, or better than eight or ten years.
Of course it's mainly the musicians that I was interested in present, but... You know, I thought you could get maybe their father's pictures. Yeah, yeah, they were in there pictures.

You see, Bob, that being her husband's daddy too, she might have had, he might have had a picture something of the grandfather, you see, then I don't know, I don't remember that. So those people have been away there, everyone's been away so long.

Is there anything else that you can tell us about this band, the Peerless band, or when they rehearsed, or anything that you can remember around the house, or did you ever get to go to their dances before they...

Well no, I never did go to their dances. I think I seen my daddy play probably, maybe six or seven times in those cabarets, go to bring him something, you know, over there, and I'd go in while I was... Those people knew me, you know, from around there, bringing his lunch and everything. And I was a small kid, I could get in there, and I've gotten there several times at night, and I was at the shop with him, working around there, cutting killing or something for him, and I'd probably go bring him something at the shop. I seen, heard him play, you know, off and on, not too many times. I doubt if it's six times that I heard him play. That is on the job, but around the house and rehearsals, I've heard him play a lot, but I mean in fuels, but I mean in those nightclubs, I've heard him play only about maybe five or six times I went to those places, you know. He was playing in a place on Liberty Street, they had a nightclub there, and he was playing in there. And I went there several times and heard him play there, but I mean I didn't hear too much of these music and dances because I was too small, I didn't go to dances, my brothers and them probably did, but I didn't.
Who was Ratty Fiend, was he, Ratty Fiend, was he related to you?

Ratty Fiend, they call him, that's the fellow you're speaking about, they must be talking about man. He was the drummer, he was the drummer, man fiend, that's who that is. In front of your half brother.

Yeah, yeah. Excuse me just a minute. Yes. Sure. Remember the last band, the very latest ones that your father worked with? You have been about twelve years old, it would be hard to remember. Yeah, I don't remember the last band.

The last time I remember seeing my father play, there was an old fellow playing, had died, and he was playing a funeral. And we was there, I was standing right in the avenue out on Clever Street, and the funeral would pass, and some part of the island, they used to call him Jean Vigne, that was the name they called him for the name, they wouldn't say Jean, they used to say Jean Vigne.
That's what I heard that name, that's what I thought might be in French.

Yeah, Jean Vigne is how they used to call me, because they were mostly like in French, you know, and when they called him, when they hollered at him, he said, I'm going to hit four more licks on this guy, he said, because someday he'll hit four on mine. And that's the last time I could remember of him playing music, you know, that I remember hearing him play. And he was beating the bass drum at the time. Yeah. And after that funeral, in fact, my brother was just older than me, we followed the funeral all the way to St. Louis graveyard. And after they got through, Baron, the man that was coming back playing, didn't he ramble, and they was carrying on him, and that was really the last time I could remember my father playing music. And then later on, he got sick, and a year later he was dead. But I don't remember the name of the band he was with when he played at the funeral, I don't remember that so well.
You remember when he died, did they have a band for his funeral too? Oh yeah.
Oh yeah. Were you all Catholics, I suppose? Catholics, yeah, we were Catholics.
At present, I don't usually, the Catholics don't favor having bands on the street for their funerals, but I just wanted to know that they did.

As of now they don't. They don't approve of it too much now. But in them times they did. They did a fun other day. Yeah, they're Catholic, they went with bands. And if they didn't want to have the band, well then they would just have the priest to bless the body at the house. And they'd go right to the graveyard. That's right. Yeah. If they didn't want to, if they just want, now my brother Sidney got killed, they might have had about seven bands behind him. Because any time a musician had died, they'd always have a band behind him. Because sometimes the wife didn't want it, didn't approve of it, you see. But most of the time they would let it go through because they knew that was his life, music and they just let music carry him away. But my father had music, I remember that well. He had maybe about two or three bands behind him. My brother had about five. He had so many of them behind him. I remember far back you could see, you could hear bands one after the other. He had a trouble as I was night, my brother Sidney was living. Oh babe, they could tell you a lot about it. Because they were, you see we have, I have about, let's see. One, two, three, four, five, six. I have about six in between my brother Sidney and I, that's how much older they were. You see if they were living, they'd be around in the, my brother Sidney would be in his seventies now if he was living. You see, yeah. And I mean they could remember everything because they were, I mean boys were big enough to be around my daddy a lot before he died around his music and all. You know they could tell you a lot about it. Then my brother played music but I was next to the baby, you see. We were nine children and I was the eighth one. So I mean that made me be real young over there under them, you see. And that's why they would know so much more than I would. Even my sisters would know more, my older sisters. But right now I got one sister older than me and she was crippled, she never did go anywhere. So I knew she wouldn't know too much. She was always home, you know she had, her hip was hurting, she used to limp and she never did go anywhere but stay in the house. So she's the only one, the only three left now and she's the only one that would be old enough to know anything. She didn't go anywhere by being crippled.

I was trying to figure if your father were living, he'd be about a hundred years old I guess. In his nineties then. Yeah. He died forty, I don't know, forty five years ago. He doesn't look close to a hundred then, wasn't he?

Yeah he would, he would. Because he died when he was around, up in his fifties. And he was dead a good forty five years ago. Because my daddy died when I was only thirteen year old. And I know that's a good forty five years ago. Because I'm fifty eight now.
Do you remember any of the cabarets that you went to to see your father play? Do you remember any that he played at?
I'll tell you where he played. You know we had a cabaret at the time? He used to play in Tom Anderson.
You know what at that place? Yeah, was that the one on Rambord Street? Or did he have a couple places?
He had one on Basin Street and one on Rambord Street. He had one on Basin Street and one on Rambord Street. He used to play. Tom Anderson on Basin Street. I remember that cabaret.
In the corner of there of the Custom House in the Basin. Yeah.

Somewhere around where Lula White's house was at. He played around there. And that was Tom Anderson. I remember hearing him saying he played at Tom Anderson when I was at Kidney Shopping. He spoke of the place where he played. I remember that place. Let's see. We had another cabaret on Liberty Street. He played in there but I can't remember the name of that place. I can't remember the name of that cabaret. In fact, I was such a young kid. I wasn't interested in there. I didn't pay much attention to those things in them days. But Tom Anderson, he played there so long and so often that I remember hearing him speak of that place, you know, around the shop, he'd speak about the place. Now they had another fellow probably you never heard talk of. You ever heard him speak of, Kokai George?
Wait a minute, I'm not sure. No.
That was a good piano player.
No, I don't think.
Kokai? Kokai George. He was cross-iron. They used to call him Kokai George, you know. He was a great piano player too. Around there.
No, I don't think so.
And then they had another boy, I guess you heard speak of him. I don't believe he was from here, but he played a lot of piano in the district and during them times. Udel.
Oh yeah, Udel Wilson. Was that the name of him?
Yeah, Udel Wilson. I remember him. He came from Kansas City. Yeah, he was a tall, brown skin boy. I knew him well.
A few people told us about him.

Yeah, well I had grown up when he was playing, that's why I knew him well, you see. He played on, right there on Franklin Street. They used to have a cabaret on Franklin. He used to play in that cabaret at night.
I remember him. The entertainers, do you remember that? I remember the entertainers. The tuxedo was on there too. You were pretty young. The villa, it was the villa by the time you came up.
Maybe the turf, I think it later changed to the turf.

I don't remember them so well. I remember the entertainers and Tom Anderson, I remember those places. But like you said, they had two, I don't know anything about the one on Rambo. I remember the one on Basin Street. I remember they had one around there, he played around there.
Is there anything you can tell us about the parades when you were a boy? What the band sounded like? Have you heard any of the parades recently within the last few years?

Yeah, I heard they have a parade around here. They have two parades every year, the Jolly Boys. And all the bands at the time when they were, my dad and them's time, I think they had a larger band. They had more big brass instruments in the band than they have now. I remember that they used to have those big brass horns and all that, very big things.
Yeah, baradones.

Yeah, in them time. But now they don't have all that. I don't see that in the bands no more. Those parades we've been having, I haven't been seeing that recently. Yeah. Not in these late years. Those fathers that played all those kind of years, we looked like they ain't got nobody want to carry nothing like that anymore.
Right. It's too big. Anything about the style of the music that's any much different or the way the parades are organized or going, anything different much in the old days if you can remember?

I don't know. I think the old days the parade was, to my eye just from what I've seen, I think they were nicer than they have now. Because the parades were, they dressed in tuxedo suits with the big pigeons on their shoulders and the big stream was down the front, you know.
The outpullers still got that.

And they had the grand marshall and they had, they called the aides on the side, they'd have maybe the grand marshall, they'd have maybe six, eight or twelve aides on the side. And they would dress something like the grand marshall, but he'd have a longer. A little fancier. A little fancier thing, I mean they had that. And they wore those, they wore those big pigeons on their shoulders, stuffed pigeons, and those high beaver hats. They don't have that in the parades now. The fellas just wear silk shirts and an umbrella and they go along dancing. It's way different from in the times when I seen parades when I was a kid, when my dad and them were playing. And they didn't have as much, the fellas do a lot of dancing and shaking in the parade. But in them days those guys just stepped proud, man. They were proud steppers, those fellas that were in the parades in them times, you know. And then they would have, they would have carriages with the horses hooked in them. And the carriages would be all decorated and they'd have batteries in them. They'd have lights all around the carriages. And oh it was pretty. And even the fellas that were in the parade would have batteries in their pockets and they'd light the pigeon up, you know, press the battery and the pigeon would light up. It was real nice in them times. Much nicer than now, the parades were anyhow. And the bands were large.
I imagine they would be better in those days. Yeah.
And then they used to, they didn't parade in the day.
They'd have night parades then. They used to parade at night.

That's why I used to have parade at night, because they had all those lights on them and those batteries and everything. And all those horses would be all decorated up with those little lights on them, battery lights. The fellas sitting in the carriage riding, they'd just press their buttons and the horses would light up, you know. All the harness and everything would light up pretty. And they'd leave it go for a certain amount of time. Then they'd put it out and maybe the next carriage he'd light up. It was real nice doing them parades they had. And then time they had the Art Fellas, they had the Bulls Club. You heard of the Bulls Club? Oh yeah. The Art Fellas, the Bulls Club, they had the Santa Sinners, and they had the Lions Club. Those were the clubs that used to parade. They used to try and outdo one another. That's what made the parade so nice. Each club would try and have a nicer parade than the other fella. Yeah. I remember those things. Well, then I'd been growing up to be a boy around about 15 or 16 year old, and them times I remember that well. But I thought the parades and them days was much nicer than that. And then we had more. Then they used to have, like say when they had a ball at a hall and it did, they would have, they'd advertise the same day of the ball. They wouldn't do like they do now, have those bills printed and put them on posts. They didn't do like that. What they did that Sunday morning, they'd get a band and they'd put it on a moving wagon, and them days they had moving wagons, a big long moving wagon with the horses. You remember those bands? Well then they'd get a band, the band that was going to play that night would get in that wagon that Sunday morning, and then they would parade all around the street in the neighborhoods to draw the people, and they would play music at each corner they'd go to, they'd play a piece. Then they'd go to the next corner and they'd play a piece. Then they'd just go all over down there, and then all in the trimmie, that's how they would advertise the dancing MVs. Of course they could afford that band at them times because those fellas didn't get but about a dollar and a half a night to play music a piece. That is the musicians, and on the truck they'd get a dollar a day to play on that truck. They would play until about, say from about nine o'clock the morning until about eleven o'clock, you see, eleven, twelve o'clock they would stop. Then they'd rest up for that night. And we'd sit in that band on the wagon, and playing at the hall that night, those fellas wouldn't even make four and a half. That's right, you could hire a band in them days for fifteen dollars. Fifteen dollars for a band. You'd give them a deposit, like say if there was going to be seven pieces, you'd give them, uh, well I guess about, let's see, seven pieces, about three and a half. Each man you'd get a sense of deposit, on the job that night.
That's what they did.
Today, when you pay one man to play now, you could get a whole band for it in them times.
Probably a better band too. Yeah. They sold it or something.

Oh, those guys, it was something. And then in the balls, they didn't, they didn't do like they do not sell all that high ball and beer and all that. When they gave a real nice ball, they sold apples, oranges, and bananas at a dance.
I've never seen that, didn't they? Yeah, they sold that at a dance.

And the girls would, went to the dance, their mothers would go over and want their grandmother. And she'd go there with a big bag and sit down on the side and she'd go up and dance. And every time she'd dance, the boy would treat her apple or banana, she'd come put it in that bag. When they leave, they had a bag of bananas.
I never heard of that.

You know what I mean? Oh yeah, that was in the old days. That's what they did, sure. That was done in the Economy Hall, the Artesian Hall, the Franz Ami. And those halls, that's what they done in those days. My sister's name is, they come out with a big bag of apples and oranges. And they'd sell those oranges, nickel apiece, and the fella danced with a girl and instead of bringing her to the boy and buy her beer, they had big crates of apples and bananas and things. He'd go there and buy an apple for them. And those things went on around, that was going on around 19, around 1918, 1970, 1920. And them times.
That was the first girl bar, how long was that period?

Yeah, that's during the time when that was going on. Because that's the time when my sister and them were young ladies and they were going to dances. And the girl didn't go to the dance like they do when I leave the house with a boy and go to the dance, come at 2 o'clock in the morning. She left with her mother or her grandmother, chaperone. Or either if the girl in these doors was going, well they both had to go with the other girl's mama. And the boys could go along with them. But the lady was with them and she'd sit there with each one of them girls' bags, their candy bags, and put them treats in there. Those kind of things went on in those days. Of course I didn't fancy much of those dances at the time. I was a little younger than my sister and then when that was going on, when I started out on the roof garden. Well, that was the later years, around up in the 20s, where they started selling highballs. And so, you know, first they were selling punch. Well, yeah, they used to sell a lot of punch at these dances too. You know, they'd treat the girls punch or they got tired drinking punch, they'd take an apple or orange, something like that. They didn't give them nothing to lose their heads like the girls are today. Yeah, they always had that chaperone.
When you were dancing, it was later than the turkey trot and dances like that, wasn't it? Or did you ever do those?

No, I was a little later than that. I was a little later than turkey trot. I didn't dance those dances. I heard of them and when I was, I imagine when I was growing up, two dancers, I'd seen them do it. They were going out with it and, you know, and like ball and jack and all that kind of stuff. I had a little before my time. I didn't do those dances.

Do you think your father ever wrote any music or, you know, did he ever have any formal training in the, some drummers, a lot of drummers are able to play, of course, without ever learning to read music. I mean, just sort of make up the parts that he ever, uh, I think my daddy read music.

He probably would. He used to read music. But I don't know of him arranging anything. But my brother arranged music and wrote music. My brother Sidney, the one who played sax, he wrote music. And you see, I was old enough when he died, got killed to remember those things. I remember seeing him sitting down and arranging music. Yeah. Yeah, he used to sit down and arrange music and write it. Yeah, he was pretty good, my brother Sidney was. But I don't remember too much about my daddy doing that, because you see, he had that business. And in the daytime he was at that business where he'd take a rest over there, he had a little room in his shop where he used to rest on the day when he was running his bed. Then at night he'd go play music, you see. So we didn't see too much of my daddy around the house, because he had a business and he played music, you see. But my brother, well he went down, but at night he was home, the nights he didn't play music, he was sitting there writing it or arranging music or something, he was pretty good at it.

Any other impressions, Russell? No. I should have mentioned on this tape in the beginning that Russell Levy is here also helping with the interviewer, this is Bill Russell, so we identify our voices on the tape in case the secretary later will be listening to this, to some of it to write down some of it. Is there anything else you'd like to add about either your life or the old times of dancing, anything else you can remember about your father or any of the other old time musicians? You did mention, I believe before we started, he played with Joe Oliver too, I think you said he worked with King Oliver.

Yeah, he worked with King Oliver. King Oliver worked with my daddy and worked with my brother. I remember King Oliver well, he was a big, heavy set dog fella, had a cataract on one eye. I remember him well, he was by my house right now, I remember him. I remember King Oliver well. And I remember Lewis Armstrong when he used to play in the yards uptown when he first started out. Now they had a picture of him when he was a boy in short pants in, what's this fella? Red, oh I can't remember, they had a place up here on Howard Street I think it was, right across from where the nightclub they got uptown there. Doudrop. Doudrop, yeah. Right across from the Doudrop they had a fella by the name of Red Batiste. And in this place, Red Batiste died, in this place they had a big frame and they had all those old time musicians in there. And even Lewis Armstrong when he was a boy in short pants.
With a trumpet or just standing there?
He was playing trumpet then. He was just starting out to play, he just got out to whom, he was playing trumpet.
I can't remember seeing those pictures, I would have been seeing them.

This man died in this place close up, I don't know who could have gotten them pictures. Red Batiste. He had a saloon right up there across from the Doudrop and the next block coming this way from the Doudrop. Because I used to go up there, we used to go up there after a dance and eat breakfast in this place. And I used to stand up there a lot of time looking at all the old musicians up there. I mean he had a size card up there. That's been a power.
That's where the housing project is in there now or is it the Shakespeare Park? I can't think.

It's in that, you know where the Shakespeare Park is at? Yeah, I know the Doudrop. Well look, going uptown, where the Shakespeare Park starts, right from that corner coming down on that side of the bay. They got several saloons along that restaurant and things, but he was right in that section there.
Right in there, yeah.
Now whoever got that place, they might have gotten them pictures when he read Batiste Died. But I mean they had a lot of pictures of musicians and different folks.
Yeah, we all tried to check on something.

And Louis Armstrong's picture was in there when he was standing up. He was standing up with a cap on like that and he's got short pants on there. You know they were short pants at them times? Yeah. And he was playing trumpet then. And when I used to go see Louis Armstrong play for, they used to have parties up there, ten cents to go in. And he used to be- The ball and burning the pitch drives and things? No, this was little matinee parties in the yard. Yeah, and they'd sell punch and stuff like that. And he had a little young band, the young fellas all playing, he was blowing trumpet. He was playing plenty of trumpet then. He was nothing but a kid. I remember, and if you see that picture, that's just like him. But he was a boy, he has never changed from a kid. Now, if y'all would have had started this, of course y'all probably had started maybe in them times. I don't know, that's been- And Baptiste is dead now, what about-
Well, yeah, I've been asked, how long ago?

But Baptiste must be dead a good ten or twelve years now. About ten or twelve years ago. But if you could have got a hold of that, that, that, that, you had everything you wanted up on there. Maybe not everything, but you had a lot on there. Yeah.
Did he have any family that you know of? Who's that? Red Baptiste. I don't know any of his people.

I just knew him from having a place up there. And having a- Now, around in that section, if you could inquire around there, maybe somebody knows people. Somebody up there would know. I never lived uptown. The only way I went up there is after a dance, we would go up that way to get a breakfast in the morning. You see, and they used to sell, they used to serve some nice breakfast up in that section, you see. And we used to go up that way and eat. And then we would come back down in our section. But the bum up there, I never lived bum up there. Just mostly go up there in the mornings like that, after a dance and have breakfast, you see. From drinking, you know, he'd like to eat something, we'd go up there and have breakfast in the morning. And that's how I come, but I know the fellow Red Baptiste, I see him at football games too. But I don't know any of these people. I don't know who was his people up there.
It's possible this picture would be someplace here, I hope. Hard to run down any good pictures usually. Very few musicians kept scrapbooks.

Now this is a picture that honestly, my daddy's picture, that's an old picture, you can see that. Now, this picture was in the latest house on St. Louis, a place where my father kept these horses. When he had his shower on, many years ago. And I found that picture up there. I seen that picture up there and I took it. And I kept the picture, I said, I'm going to take this picture, I said, that's my daddy on there. And I kept the picture away from him and I carried it to my house. And I've been nursing that picture ever since. And that's been many years ago. And I just kept that picture and saved it, you know, just because he was on it. It's a good picture. And my sisters never wanted it. And they said, let it to me, I'm going to have some men like it, I want to get one of it. You know, after you get to a certain age, you can, my sister's younger than me, she doesn't remember my dad as well as I did, you see. I want to get his picture made. And I went on and I promised to tell her, but I never did give it to her. And then I loaned it to her one time, at the time of year again. She bent it in half. Bent it in half and everything else. That's why I never didn't want to give it to her. Well, at that time she wouldn't get the picture made. I know she wanted it for something. She'd come in, she'd beg, but she said, I'll take it, I'll bring it back. I said, all right. Then when you came, it wasn't here, I had to go get it for me. You remember that?
Yeah. Well, I glued it back together. It's in shape again.

Well, we have another one now. And now my sister was here today. She saw the large medium. She said, well, where did you get that at? She said, don't you have another one? I said, I have the old one. Well, what do you want to do with two of them? Now she's trying to get one, you see. Yeah, we'll give it that one. No, this one's for my little sister.
Oh, that's the other one. That's the younger sister. I'll get you another print. I have another print. I'm Kevin.
